sentences.text: This species is smaller than the smallest known members of its close relative, Confuciusornis.
Unlike some relatives, the bone ridge on its upper arm bone lacks a hole.
The fossil shows two long, ribbon-like tail feathers similar to those seen in male relatives.
Evidence suggests a head crest resembling modern turacos, though this feature might be a conservation artifact.
In 1998, researchers Ji Shuan and Luis Chiappe identified a specimen of Confuciusornis that appeared distinct from others in the National Geological Museum of China.
In 1999, Ji, Chiappe, and Ji Qiang formally named the species Changchengornis hengdaoziensis.
The main specimen was found near the village of Jianshangou in Liaoning province within the Jianshangou Beds of the Hengdaozi Member.
This largely complete skeleton is preserved as a compressed plate and counterplate.
Much of the feathering on this specimen is preserved in an excellent state.
In 1999, Changchengornis was assigned to the family Confuciusornithidae.
Remains of Changchengornis have been found in the Chaomidianzi Formation in China, dating to the Barremian-Aptian boundary approximately 125 million years ago.
The time range for Changchengornis is the Barremian to Aptian, spanning from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
